Performers
Isaac Stern (violin), Alexander Schneider (violin), Milton Katims (viola), Pablo Casals (cello), Paul Tortelier (cello) Documented

The Internet Archive item lists these five performers as creators; the Substack essay assigns the roles and calls the recording a Columbia release made at the Prades Festival. Which cellist plays the first cello part and which the second is not stated in any source consulted.

[1] [4]
Work version
Unknown Unknown

The performing edition is not identified. The Internet Archive file names print the posthumous opus number 163 for the work, which Schubert’s catalogue gives as D. 956.

[1] [3]
Recorded
1952 (the Casals Festival at Prades); one secondary source says July Documented

The LP sleeve notes say the recordings were made in Prades during the Casals Festival of 1952; the Discogs master release and a 6moons review also say 1952. Only the Substack essay by John Buxton gives a month, July 1952, so the month is not treated as established, and the day is not stated.

[2] [3] [5] [4]
Place
Prades, France (Prades Festival); the venue within Prades is not identified Documented

The sleeve notes say the recordings were made in Prades during the Casals Festival of 1952. Substack says the recording was made in Prades, France during the Prades Festival; Discogs and 6moons say it was recorded at the Prades Festival in 1952.

[2] [4] [3] [5]
Label
Columbia Masterworks Documented

The label is the item’s publisher metadata and the title shown on its page.

[1]
Catalogue
ML 4714 / SL-183, Casals Festival at Prades, Third Series Documented

The Internet Archive item page prints “Columbia Masterworks (ML 4714 / SL-183)” with publication date 1953. A 1976 CBS Classics reissue (61043) and a Philips issue (A 01188 L) are listed on Discogs and are not this carrier.

[1]
Matrix, take, sides
Side 1, second track of the LP (file 01.02 on the Internet Archive); matrix and take numbers are not established Unknown

The Internet Archive file for the Adagio is a derivative linked to a segments file, so the cut between the first movement and the Adagio is the Internet Archive’s. No matrix or take numbers appear in the sources consulted.

[1]
Transfer
Internet Archive LP digitisation: ripped by an Internet Archive associate at the Cebu scanning centre (rip station archivelp-rip-cebu04); the cover was scanned and the item created by another associate Documented

The item metadata names a ripping operator and a ripping scanner, a scanning centre (cebu) and a separate scanning operator. The item is listed in several vinyl collections, including the Boston Public Library’s; which physical copy was digitised is not stated.

[1]
Transfer date
4 January 2021 (the ripping date recorded in the item metadata) Documented

The metadata gives ripping_date 20210104123741. The artwork scan date and public date are 24 November 2020 and the added date is 4 January 2021; these are separate events and the scan and upload dates are not transfer dates.

[1]
Processing
Technics SL1200MK5 turntable with Audio-⁠Technica AT95e cartridge, Radio Design Labs EZ-PH1 phono preamp and Focusrite Scarlett 2i2 interface; the Adagio file is an MP3 derivative of the side Documented

The hardware chain is the lineage field of the item metadata; the file inventory also reports generic SoX processing of the side files, with no settings. The equalisation curve, noise treatment, original recording engineering and playing-speed accuracy are not documented and are not inferred from the equipment names.

[1]
Composition rights
Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies. Inferred, not documented

Schubert died in 1828. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about an unidentified modern edition.

[6] [7]
Recording rights
Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis). Documented

The Internet Archive item gives publication date 1953 and the Discogs master release gives the year 1953, so the 50-year European term expired before the 2013 extension. The item carries no licence statement; no US public-domain basis is claimed, and the 1953 date is not independently verified against a label image.

  • Pre-1963 European public domain — territorial basis, publication 1953.
  • No licence or rights statement on the Internet Archive item.

Franz Schubert, String Quintet in C major, D. 956, II. Adagio; Isaac Stern and Alexander Schneider, violins, Milton Katims, viola, Pablo Casals and Paul Tortelier, cellos; Prades Festival, 1952. Columbia Masterworks ML 4714 / SL-183, 1953; Internet Archive LP digitisation. Public domain in the EU only (pre-1963 publication); no worldwide recording clearance is asserted. Rights statement

LP sleeve notes — Casals Festival at Prades, Third Series (Columbia Masterworks), as OCR text on the Internet Archive — Sleeve text: “The recordings, made in Prades during the Casals Festival of 1952, are devoted to the chamber music of Schubert, Schumann and Brahms”; the Schubert Quintet in C major, Op. 163, with Stern, Schneider, Katims, Casals and Tortelier listed on the sleeve; note on the Adagio citing Einstein.. Accessed 2026-10-17.

John Buxton — Building a Collection #24: Schubert’s String Quintet in C major — “The Essential Recording”: recorded by Columbia Records in July 1952 in Prades, France during the Prades Festival; players Stern (then 32), Schneider, Katims, Tortelier and Casals; Casals’s grunting audible in several places; quotes Jonathan Blumhofer’s programme note.. Accessed 2026-10-17.
  5. 6moons — Casals & friends play Schubert’s String Quintet in C Major D956 — Review of the Sony Classical Casals Edition CD: the quintet “was recorded at the Prades festival in 1952”, with Stern, Schneider, Casals, Tortelier and Katims.. Accessed 2026-10-17.
  6. Wikipedia — Franz Schubert — Lead paragraph: 31 January 1797 – 19 November 1828.. Accessed 2026-10-17.
  7. Directive 2006/116/EC — copyright term — Articles 1(1) and 8: life plus 70 years, calculated from the following 1 January; national exceptions and editions require separate consideration.. Accessed 2026-10-17.
  8. Directive 2011/77/EU — transitional sound-recording term — Article 1(3), inserting Article 10(5): the extended term applies to phonograms still protected on 1 November 2013.. Accessed 2026-10-17.
